lessons.title: When Great Businesses Became Poor Investments

body.text: The company can do everything right and the shareholder can still earn nothing. A business compounds earnings. A shareholder compounds earnings multiplied by whatever the market decides to pay for them.

children.text: This lesson is the necessary companion to the last one. Every example here is a genuinely excellent business with a real moat, strong returns on capital, and growing earnings. In each case, investors who bought at the wrong price waited years, sometimes more than a decade, to make money. None of them was wrong about the company.
The Three Ways a Great Business Disappoints

body.caption: How a quality investment can go wrong without the moat failing

cells: Earnings keep growing but the market pays less per rupee of them, so the price stagnates or falls
Typically 3 to 10 years, until earnings grow into the old valuation
The business grows well, but slower than the price assumed, so the multiple corrects to match reality
Permanent: the lost value is never recovered, only grown past
Returns decline gradually while the market still pays a premium for past quality
Permanent, and the worst of the three, because both earnings and the multiple fall

body.text: Only the third is a failure of moat analysis. The first two are failures of price discipline, which is why an investor can become expert at identifying moats and still perform poorly. Chapters 1 to 6 were necessary. They were not sufficient.

children.text: The Arithmetic of Waiting

Take a company that compounds earnings at 14.0% a year, an excellent record by any standard. You buy it at 65 times earnings. Over the years that follow, its multiple settles at 35 times, which is still a healthy premium for a quality business. Here is what you earn, depending on how long you hold.

body.title: Annual Return vs Earnings Growth at Different Holding Periods (%)

stats.label: After 5 years
stats.context: Total gain of just 3.7% over the whole period

stats.label: After 10 years
stats.context: The derating is spread over twice as long

stats.label: After 15 years
stats.context: Approaching the company's own earnings growth

children.text: Five years of 14.0% earnings growth produced almost nothing for the shareholder, because the multiple nearly halved. The business did not disappoint. The entry price did. And notice the pattern: the longer you hold, the closer your return moves towards the company's earnings growth, exactly as Chapter 1 predicted. Time is the antidote to overpaying, but only if the moat survives the wait.

body.title: Calculate the Damage
body.prompt: You buy a company at 50 times earnings. Over the next five years its earnings grow 15% a year, but the multiple falls to 30 times. What is your annual return, in percent?
body.explanation: Earnings grow 1.15^5 = 2.01 times. The multiple changes by 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60. Price factor = 2.01 × 0.60 = 1.21. Annual return = 1.21^(1/5) − 1 = 3.8%. Five years of excellent operating performance, and you earned less than a fixed deposit would have paid.

children.text: Three Episodes Worth Knowing

body.title: Quality bought at the wrong price

events.title: The American Nifty Fifty
events.description: A group of large, genuinely dominant US companies were treated as one-decision stocks that could be bought at any price. Many traded above 50 times earnings. Most remained excellent businesses, but investors who bought at the peak waited many years to recover, because the multiples came down as interest rates rose.

events.title: Indian IT at the dot-com peak
events.description: Leading Indian software companies were superb businesses with real switching costs and high returns on capital. At the top of the technology boom they traded at extraordinary multiples. Earnings continued to compound through the 2000s, but shareholders who bought at the peak spent years underwater despite owning the right companies.

events.title: The Indian quality derating
events.description: Several leading consumer and technology companies, bought heavily during the pandemic rally for their safety and quality, saw multiples compress over the following two years while earnings grew steadily. Nothing changed about their moats. The market simply repriced how much it would pay for them.

body.text: A common thread runs through all three episodes: a widely shared belief that price does not matter for truly great companies. That belief always appears near the end of a rerating, never near the start. When you hear "you can never overpay for quality", the arithmetic in this lesson is the answer.

body.title: Why multiples compress even when nothing goes wrong

children.text: Interest rates rise:
a higher cost of equity reduces the value of distant cash flows, and high-multiple stocks hold most of their value in distant years. This is arithmetic, not sentiment.
Growth expectations normalise:
a company growing 20% is often priced as if it always will. When growth settles at 12%, the multiple settles with it.
Flows reverse:
concentrated buying from funds, index inclusion, or a popular theme can lift a multiple beyond fundamentals, and the same flows can unwind.
Competition arrives:
even without denting current earnings, a credible new entrant lowers the certainty premium the market pays.
Notice that only the last relates to the moat. Three of the four are about the market, not the business, which is why an investor who analyses only the company is blindsided.
Warning Signs That You Are Overpaying
Implied growth exceeds historical growth:
run the reverse calculation from the last lesson. If the price implies faster growth than the company has ever achieved, you are paying for an improvement, not a record.
The multiple is far above its own long-run median:
compare today's P/E with the company's 10-year median on Screener.in. A stock at twice its own median needs a specific, evidenced reason.
The rerating came without a change in fundamentals:
if ROCE, margins, and growth look the same as three years ago but the multiple has doubled, the market changed its mind, not the business.
Justifications shift to non-financial arguments:
when the case rests on brand strength or market position alone, with no reference to price, the discipline has quietly been abandoned.
Everyone agrees:
a universally admired company with no bearish view in sight usually has that admiration already in the price.

body.label: The uncomfortable truth
body.value: Identifying a moat correctly guarantees nothing about your return
body.context: Your return is the moat's earnings growth multiplied by the change in what the market pays for it. You control only the price you pay.

body.title: Diagnose the Disappointment
body.question: You bought a wide-moat company four years ago. Since then its revenue has grown 12% a year, ROCE has stayed at 29%, market share has edged up, and the stock is down 8% in total. What most likely happened?
options: The moat eroded and you should sell
The multiple compressed from a high starting level, so the business performed while the valuation corrected
The market has made a permanent error you should ignore
body.explanation: Every operating indicator improved, which rules out moat erosion and misallocation. Growing earnings with a falling price means only one thing: the multiple fell. Whether to hold now depends on today's implied growth and your rescored moat, not on your purchase price, which is irrelevant to the decision ahead.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: The longer you hold a moat business bought at a high multiple, the closer your annual return moves towards the company's ___ growth.
body.explanation: A one-time derating is spread across more years the longer you hold, so its annual drag shrinks. This only works if the moat lasts through the holding period.

body.title: Three Years Underwater
body.scenario: You bought a listed branded consumer company three years ago at 68 times earnings. Since then: earnings have grown 11% a year, ROCE has held near 30%, volume growth has slowed from 8% to 3% while price-led growth has risen, a well-funded competitor has entered the category, and the stock is roughly flat. It now trades at 49 times earnings. Your scorecard has moved from 21 to 18 out of 24.
body.prompt: What should drive your decision now, and what would you do?
body.modelAnswer: Start by discarding the purchase price, which is a sunk cost and tells you nothing about future returns. The decision rests on two current questions. First, what does 49 times imply? Using the reverse calculation, a multiple this high still assumes sustained high growth and returns for a very long time. Second, what does the evidence say? The scorecard has fallen three points, and the reason matters: volume growth slowing to 3% with growth increasingly price-led is a leading indicator of a narrowing moat, and a funded competitor is exactly the kind of entrant that tests pricing power. So this is not the benign case in the quiz, where only the multiple fell. Here the multiple fell and the leading indicators weakened at the same time, which suggests the derating was at least partly justified. What I would do: trim rather than exit, since the moat remains strong at 18 of 24 and ROCE is intact; write down the two specific indicators I am tracking, volume growth and gross margin, with a threshold that would trigger a further reduction; and stop anchoring to the 68 times entry, since hoping to get back to the purchase price is the single most expensive habit in quality investing.

body.title: Pre-Purchase Price Discipline
steps: Write down the company's 10-year median P/E from Screener.in and compare it with today's multiple
Calculate the growth implied by the current price using the method from the previous lesson
Compare that implied growth with the company's actual five and ten-year earnings growth
Estimate your return if the multiple reverts to the median over five years, holding your growth estimate
If that return is below what a fixed deposit would pay, decide whether the moat justifies waiting longer
Set your position size and tranche plan before buying, not after the first fall

body.text: Historical episodes are described in general terms from widely reported market history for teaching purposes, without company-specific price data or recommendations. All calculations use hypothetical figures. Past patterns do not predict future outcomes.

points: A great business can be a poor investment through multiple compression, growth below what the price implied, or unpriced moat erosion
Only the third is a failure of moat analysis; the first two are failures of price discipline
At 14% earnings growth with a multiple falling from 65 to 35 times, a five-year holding returns about 0.7% a year
The longer the holding period, the closer returns move towards earnings growth, provided the moat survives
Multiples compress for reasons unrelated to the business: rates, normalising expectations, and reversing flows
Your purchase price is a sunk cost; every decision from here depends on today's implied assumptions and today's scorecard
